clue.text: Grown-up girl wedded to crime

parts.note: a grown-up is big
a girl's name

explanation.surface: A grown woman has married into a life of crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wedded' sounds like part of the story and also hints at the answer, the crime of being married twice over.
explanation.definitionFit: Bigamy, marrying while already married, is a criminal offence in most countries.

clue.text: Newly-wed occupied by mounting tick? That's commonplace!

definitions.note: a phrase standing for the noun: a commonplace remark

indicators.note: something occupied has another thing living inside it, so one word sits within the other

parts.note: a woman just married

indicators.note: in a down entry, mounting means climbing, so the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a tick is a moment, MO for short

explanation.surface: A newly married person finds a tick crawling up them, and shrugs it off as ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tick' looks like the insect, but it is the short moment as in 'just a tick'; the exclamation is the definition, a dull remark.
explanation.definitionFit: A bromide is a trite, unoriginal remark, a platitude, originally from the sedative drug's dulling effect.

clue.text: Sudden burst of wind — not something that gives pleasure!

parts.note: a brief rush of wind
read as nought, the zero-shaped letter

explanation.surface: A sudden blast of wind is described as no fun at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash and 'not' make it look like a negative comment on wind, but 'not' supplies the round letter and the rest is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Gusto is keen enjoyment or relish, the zest that makes eating or doing something a delight.

clue.text: Assembly retaining the North, ie the Province

indicators.note: to retain is to keep hold of, so one word holds the other within it

parts.note: a gathering of troops for inspection
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A gathering keeps a northern perspective, as befits the regional authority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Province' usually means Northern Ireland, but here it is one of the four historic provinces of Ireland, in the south-west.
explanation.definitionFit: Munster is one of Ireland's four traditional provinces, covering Cork, Kerry, Limerick and neighbouring counties.

clue.text: Descriptive of surface of leather or pelt

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a grainy textured finish on leather
second meaning: to pelt someone with small stones

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pelt' looks like a noun meaning an animal skin, which fits the leather surface; it is really the verb to bombard.
explanation.definitionFit: Leather is pebbled when given a bumpy grain, and to pebble a target is to throw small stones at it.

clue.text: Top businessman I see quitting

indicators.note: whatever is quitting leaves, so those letters drop out of the word

parts.note: a senior manager in a company
taken as written
v. abbreviates vide, Latin for see

explanation.surface: A senior executive says he is leaving the company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like it describes the businessman; it is the definition, slang for kill. Removing I and V from EXECUTIVE leaves EXECUTE.
explanation.definitionFit: To top someone is British slang for killing them, as an executioner puts a condemned person to death.

clue.text: RA blessed, perhaps, in not having a Vandyke

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters are only one possible arrangement, to be tried in another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A blessed Royal Academician, perhaps a portrait painter, lacks the famous pointed beard.
explanation.walkthrough: Van Dyck was a painter, which fits the RA (Royal Academician) of the surface; a Vandyke is the short pointed beard seen in his portraits.
explanation.definitionFit: A Vandyke is a type of beard, so someone without one may be clean-shaven, lacking facial hair.

clue.text: I fly high, say, to see this sight

indicators.note: say asks for the words to be spoken, keeping their sound but not their spelling

parts.note: to soar is to fly high

explanation.surface: Someone soaring aloft looks down on a view below.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sight' looks like the view from on high; in its colloquial sense it means something ugly.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling something a sight means it looks unattractive or ridiculous, exactly what an ugly building is.

clue.text: Formality shown — find a way to bend

parts.note: St is short for street, a way
to arch is to curve or bend

explanation.surface: Stiff manners are on display, so someone must learn to unbend.
explanation.definitionFit: Starch figuratively means stiffness of manner, the stuffy correctness of very formal behaviour.

clue.text: The Highland fling

parts.note: surface reading: a lively Scottish folk dance
setter's reading: a literal throw at the Highland Games, of a heavy pole

explanation.walkthrough: The Highland fling is a well-known dance; read literally, it is the famous throwing event of Scottish Highland Games.
explanation.definitionFit: This Scottish sport involves hurling a long wooden pole end over end, a literal Highland throw.

clue.text: Dress right — one must have Parisian taste

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
the Roman numeral for one
goût is French for taste

explanation.surface: Advice on dressing correctly: a person needs Parisian flair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dress' looks like a verb, but it is the noun the answer means.
explanation.definitionFit: A rig-out is an informal British word for an outfit or set of clothes.

clue.text: Attacks with shells — no retreat!

parts.note: rounds of ammunition

indicators.note: a retreat is a going backwards, so the word runs right to left

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An army bombards the enemy with artillery and refuses to fall back.
explanation.walkthrough: The military surface makes 'attacks' sound literal; the answer means to turn on someone verbally.
explanation.definitionFit: To round on someone is to turn and attack them suddenly, usually with angry words.

clue.text: Career's involved hard study

indicators.note: involved means intricate or tangled, so the letters are mixed up together

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Someone's career has demanded long, difficult study.
explanation.definitionFit: Research is detailed investigation of a subject, the systematic study of sources to establish facts.

clue.text: Stir, before taking this drink

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sensation, a revelation that causes surprise
second meaning: a morning drink taken to wake oneself up

explanation.surface: Instructions say to stir a cocktail before drinking it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stir' reads as a mixing instruction but is the noun for a commotion; 'before taking this' hints at the first drink of the day.
explanation.definitionFit: A startling revelation is called this, and in America so is an early alcoholic pick-me-up.

clue.text: Old boy's lost capital in the city

indicators.note: the capital is the opening capital letter, and losing it drops that first letter

parts.note: ex means former
a boy's name

explanation.surface: A former pupil has lost his money while living in the city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old boy' looks like one phrase, a former pupil; it splits into old and boy. Capital suggests money but means the first letter. Exeter is the county town of Devon.
explanation.definitionFit: Exeter is a cathedral city in south-west England, the county town of Devon.

clue.text: Cannon's part responsible for reported gap in defences

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so its sound counts, not its spelling

parts.note: a breach is a gap broken in a wall or defensive line

explanation.surface: A cannon is blamed for blowing a hole in the fortifications.
explanation.definitionFit: The breech is the rear end of a gun barrel, where the charge is loaded in a cannon.

clue.text: Port, in our view, makes one boisterous

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro, a Brazilian port
as it seems to us

explanation.surface: We reckon drinking port makes a person rowdy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' suggests the fortified wine in a drinking scene; it is a harbour city.
explanation.definitionFit: Riotous behaviour is wild, noisy and unrestrained, much like boisterous merrymaking.

clue.text: Shire, say, keeping name given to a place in Yorkshire

indicators.note: keeping means holding on to, so one word holds the other inside it

parts.note: the Shire is a breed of heavy draught horse; say marks it as an example
N is the abbreviation for name
taken as written

explanation.surface: A county keeps a name for one of its Yorkshire towns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shire' looks like a county, fitting Yorkshire, but it is the horse breed. Hornsea is a seaside town on the East Yorkshire coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Hornsea is a small coastal resort town in the East Riding of Yorkshire, known for its pottery.

clue.text: Plants take fish unloaded here, perhaps

parts.note: docks are broad-leaved weeds
the ide is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: Factories take delivery of fish landed at this spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plants' suggests factories, but means docks the weeds; 'fish' does double duty in the surface as the cargo being landed.
explanation.definitionFit: Cargo is unloaded from ships at the quay, the area beside the docks where vessels moor.

clue.text: One probing Minister was first set up

indicators.note: in a down entry, set up means raised, so the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: Rev., short for Reverend, a minister of religion
to have led is to have been in front

explanation.surface: An investigator reveals the minister was the first to be framed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set up' hints at framing someone; it reverses REV LED.
explanation.definitionFit: A delver digs into things, figuratively someone who researches or investigates deeply.

clue.text: Country house serving two kinds of beverage, you say

parts.note: cha (char) is British slang for tea
the second kind, the standard word

indicators.note: say asks for the word to be spoken, so a letter that sounds the same will do

parts.note: the letter U is pronounced like this word

explanation.surface: A stately home offers guests a choice of drinks, says the host.
explanation.walkthrough: The two beverages are both tea, under two names.
explanation.definitionFit: A château is a French castle or large country residence, typically on a wine estate.

clue.text: Put on fancy wear and brag?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to wear a costume or smart clothes
second meaning: to embellish, make something sound better than it is

explanation.surface: Someone puts on fine clothes and shows off.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that 'brag' is a loose match: to dress up a story is to boast by embellishing it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb covers donning a costume and also exaggerating or embellishing facts boastfully.

clue.text: Form of punishment exposed by one bearing stripes

definitions.note: the adjective in the phrase corporal punishment, not a noun

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a junior army rank with two chevrons on the sleeve

explanation.surface: A soldier with stripes reveals a type of punishment, perhaps one that leaves stripes of its own.
explanation.walkthrough: Stripes suggest the marks left by a cane; here they are sleeve chevrons of rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporal punishment means physical beating, and a corporal is a non-commissioned officer wearing two chevrons.

clue.text: Sharpness shown in a document's contents, overlooking nothing

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to overlook something is to leave it out, so that letter is removed
the contents of a word are what lies inside it, dropping its first and last letters

parts.note: the word document without its outer letters
the zero-shaped letter

explanation.surface: A shrewd mind is evident in what a document contains, missing nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overlooking nothing' sounds like thoroughness, but tells you to drop the O from the inner letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Acumen is keen insight and shrewd judgement, the mental sharpness of a quick-witted person.

clue.text: Place in South Africa, not its capital city

definitions.note: an adjective for the noun: of a city

indicators.note: the capital of a word is its first letter, and not having it means dropping that letter

parts.note: a port city on South Africa's east coast

explanation.surface: A South African town that is not the nation's capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' tempts you toward Pretoria or Cape Town; it means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Urban describes things belonging to towns and cities, as in an urban area or city life.

clue.text: Go flat out?

parts.note: surface reading: run at top speed, give it everything
setter's reading: go as do, flat as level, out as utmost, piece by piece

explanation.walkthrough: Each word of the clue has a twin in the answer phrase: go matches do, flat matches level, and out (to the utmost) the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: Trying as hard as possible is what giving maximum effort, going flat out, really means.

clue.text: Screech or hoot?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a loud piercing cry
second meaning: someone or something hilariously funny

explanation.walkthrough: Screech and hoot together suggest owls; hoot is really the informal word for a very funny thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A scream is a shrill cry, and informally a person or event that is extremely amusing.

clue.text: Knock back drink after eating game with veg

indicators.note: back tells you the whole construction is turned to read in the opposite direction
whatever is eating takes the other inside itself

parts.note: a pint of beer
RU is rugby union

explanation.surface: Someone downs a pint after a meal of game birds and vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knock back drink' reads as downing a pint, but knock back is the reversal signal and applies to the whole assembly, game inserted included.
explanation.definitionFit: A turnip is a root vegetable, white-fleshed and commonly boiled or mashed.
